title: Leave Jason Arday Alone – This Is a Scandal of Academic Educational Leadership
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Stephen Vainker argues that the focus on Jason Arday's academic misconduct—and the racially charged criticism surrounding it—obscures the deeper scandal, which is an institutional failure of educational leadership to preserve the field's core purpose: generating knowledge that improves classroom practice. Drawing parallels with his documented case against John Hattie and BERA's publication of AI-generated research, Vainker identifies a systemic pattern: academic stars are protected by their institutions not because their work is rigorous but because it is politically and reputationally useful. Managerialism, diversity metrics, and prestige-seeking have combined to produce a field that is simultaneously high-status and increasingly detached from the realities of teaching and learning.
points: The Arday integrity scandal is primarily a failure of academic institutional leadership, not an individual moral failure—and the racially charged framing of most criticism actively obscures the systemic issue.
Vainker's thesis: educational academia has lost its primary purpose (improving education) and been captured by politicized metrics, prestige-seeking, and managerialism.
Both Hattie and Arday illustrate the same structural dynamic: stars are protected by institutions because they are reputationally and politically valuable, not because their work withstands scrutiny.

Managerialism produces four specific pathologies in educational research: detachment from classroom practice, facile implications, derivative theory, and hiring on identity markers over academic merit.
The scandal Vainker identifies is not that Arday made mistakes but that institutional leaders are more interested in strategic positioning than in restoring the field's substantive purpose.
quotes: Jason Arday absolutely doesn't deserve all the nasty criticism. He was a young scholar trying to make his way, and like lots of us but more so, made huge mistakes in search of the prize of a successful academic career.

The real significance of the Arday case is that it serves as a further demonstration that the field of educational academia has lost a sense of its primary, substantive purpose: to generate and share knowledge that will improve education.

This managerialism has perverse consequences. Not only is research judged against spurious measures of quality and impact, but academia is judged against broader social metrics, including those related to diversity and inclusion, that may very well serve to distract from or supersede academic issues.
The leaders in the field do not seem to be interested in putting the field back on track—they are more concerned with following what is strategically useful to maintaining their status.

Hattie and Arday are both stars valuable to the reputation of the university, so they were protected. In both cases, the important aspect is not related to the specific research agenda, but to political usefulness for the institution.
